title: The blessing that names no side
hookLine: her son asks for a blessing to win, and Gandhari blesses dharma instead
carry: where dharma is, there is victory
last: VANAPRASTHA: A SEASON FOR LETTING GO.

lines: A SON ASKS FOR A BLESSING.
cards: A mother's blessing, before a fight, is supposed to be easy. Go well. Come home.
Win. During the war, the Mahabharata says, Duryodhana came to his mother Gandhari and asked for her blessing for victory. He was her son.
He was fighting for his life and his crown. All she had to say was, may you win. She never said it.
Today Gandhari gets her own days, starting with the words she gave him instead.

teach.h: WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY
teach.b: Her answer is a short line in Sanskrit: yato dharmas tato jayah. Where dharma is, there is victory. It's a blessing that refuses to take sides by name.
If Duryodhana is in the right, it's a blessing. If he isn't, it's a warning. And it wasn't the first time she said hard things to him.

teach.h: SHE WARNS HIM IN OPEN COURT
teach.b: Before the war, in the Book of Effort, she is called into the royal court while Krishna's peace mission is failing.
She speaks to her son in front of everyone, in paraphrase: a person who can't rule his own senses can't rule a kingdom for long. Make peace with your cousins. Duryodhana walks out of the hall.
Here's the teaching under both scenes.

Dharma, the right order of things, stands above my side and your side, even above a mother's love for her son. Gandhari doesn't stop being his mother; she just won't pray for anything but what's right.
And the line outlives her. After the war, when grief makes her want to curse the victors, the epic reminds her of her own words.

teach.h: THE MOTTO OF INDIA'S SUPREME COURT
teach.b: Today, yato dharmas tato jayah is the motto of the Supreme Court of India, written on its emblem: a mother's answer before a battle, now over the country's highest court.
And it's how many Hindu families pray before an exam, a match, a court date: not just let me win, but let what's right win, and let me be on that side.

how: Hindus hear Gandhari's words in retellings of the Mahabharata; the phrase yato dharmas tato jayah is the motto of the Supreme Court of India.

o: the mother who blesses dharma, not her son's side
a queen who curses her own son before battle
a mother who blesses her son to win at any cost

p: asks for a blessing to win
carries her line as its motto

s: Gandhari blessed Duryodhana: may you win
she said only: where dharma is, there is victory.
before the war, Gandhari spoke to her son in open court and urged peace
she told him one who can't rule his own senses can't rule a kingdom for long.
Gandhari's line names the Pandavas as the righteous side
it names no side: dharma stands above any side, even a mother's.

games.q: you're Gandhari. your son, fighting for his life, asks for your blessing for victory. what do you say?
o: where dharma is, there is victory.
games.why: she gives a blessing that names no side. after the war, her own words are recalled to her when grief tempts her to curse.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love who is pushing hard for something right now, and notice the easy blessing you'd like to give: go on, you'll win.

Then, the way Gandhari did, wish for what's right instead, in your own plain words: may what's right win, and may they be on that side. Stay with that wish for a few breaths. If you pray, you can pray it for them.

wordCard.voice: Gandhari. Asked by her son for a blessing of victory, she said only: where dharma is, there is victory. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: where dharma is, there is victory. Gandhari's answer to Duryodhana.

carryVoice: Your line: where dharma is, there is victory. Gandhari blessed what was right, not her son's side. That's today, done.
